Date and time (UTC): Maiden flight of Falcon Heavy, using two recovered Falcon 9 cores as side boosters (from the Thaicom 8[244] and SpaceX CRS-9[123] missions), as well as a modified Block 3 booster reinforced to endure the additional load from the two side boosters. The static fire test, held on 24 January 2018, was the first time 27 engines were tested together.[245] The launch was a success, and the side boosters landed simultaneously at adjacent ground pads.[246] This was the first ever use of SpaceX Landing Zone 2. Drone ship landing of the central core failed due to TEA–TEB chemical igniter running out, preventing two of its engines from restarting; the landing failure caused damage to the nearby drone ship.[247][248] Final burn to heliocentric Earth-Mars orbit was performed after the second stage and payload cruised for 6 hours through the Van Allen radiation belts.[249] Later, Elon Musk tweeted that the third burn was successful,[250] and JPL Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System showed the second stage and payload in an orbit with an aphelion of 1.67 AU.[251] The live webcast proved immensely popular, as it became the second most watched livestream so far on YouTube, reaching over 2.3 million concurrent views.[252] Over 100,000 visitors are believed to have come to the Space Coast to watch the launch in person.[253](more details)

Date and time (UTC): Last flight of a Block 3 first stage. Reused the booster from the Formosat-5 mission.[255] Paz (peace) is Spain's first spy satellite[256] that will be operated in a constellation with the German SAR fleet TSX and TDX.[257] In addition, the rocket carried two SpaceX test satellites for their forthcoming communications network in low Earth orbit.[258][259] This core flew without landing legs and was expended at sea.[258] It also featured an upgraded payload fairing 2.0 with a first recovery attempt using the Mr. Steven crew boat equipped with a net. The fairing narrowly missed the boat, but achieved a soft water landing.[260][261][262]

Date and time (UTC): The Spanish commsat was the largest satellite yet flown by SpaceX, "nearly the size of a bus".[268] A drone ship landing was planned, but scrapped due to unfavorable weather conditions. After stage separation, the first stage booster successfully conducted an ocean landing in the Atlantic Ocean.[269] SpaceX left the landing legs and titanium grid fins in place to prevent further delays, after previous concerns with the fairing pressurization and conflicts with the Atlas V launch of GOES-S.[270] The Hispasat 30W-6 satellite was propelled into a supersynchronous transfer orbit.[271]

As with recent reflown boosters, SpaceX used the controlled descent of the first stage to test more booster recovery options.[274][275] SpaceX planned a second recovery attempt of one half of the fairing using the specially modified boat Mr. Steven,[276] but the parafoil twisted, which led to the fairing half missing the boat.[277]

Date and time (UTC): First NASA high-priority science mission launched by SpaceX. Part of the Explorers program, TESS is space telescope intended for wide-field search of exoplanets transiting nearby stars. It was the first time SpaceX launched a scientific satellite which wasn't designed to focus on Earth observations. The second stage placed the spacecraft into a high elliptical Earth orbit, after which the satellite performed its own maneuvers, including a lunar flyby, such that over the course of two months it reached a stable 2:1 resonant orbit with the Moon.[293] In January 2018, SpaceX received NASA's Launch Services Program Category 2 certification of its Falcon 9 "Full Thrust", certification which is required for launching "medium-risk" missions like TESS.[294] Last launch of a new Block 4 booster,[295] and the 24th successful recovery of the first stage. An experimental water landing of the launch fairing was performed in order to attempt fairing recovery, primarily as a test of parachute systems.[292][290]

Date and time (UTC): First CRS mission with the Falcon 9 Block 5. This carried the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation lidar (GEDI) as an external payload.[362] The mission was delayed by one day due to moldy rodent food for one of the experiments on the Space Station. A previously flown Dragon spacecraft was used for the mission. The booster, in use for the first time, experienced a grid fin hydraulic pump stall on reentry, which caused it to spin out of control and touchdown at sea, heavily damaging the interstage section; this was the first failed landing targeted for a ground pad.[363][364]
